title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
body: Crime India Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight? Seerat Chabba in New Delhi 10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back in the 1990s. https://p.dw.com/p/5OrDd Prefer DW on Google Indian actor Tiger Shroff (center) was recently shot at in Mumbai [FILE March 17, 2017] Image: Amal KS/Hindustan Times/IMAGO Advertisement "In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed." This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting. The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement. The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood" . Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000). The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe , with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times. For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago. When the underworld ruled Bollywood In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry. "The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades. Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood. During his era, Dawood Ibrahim has been one of the most wanted men in India Image: AP Photo/picture alliance To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added. When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded. Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings. D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands. Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons. "A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts. By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging. A gang run from a prison cell The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai. Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab." "He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW. Lawrence Bishnoi was a student politician in the northern city of Chandigarh before gaining notoriety as a gangster Image: Sameer Sehgal/Hindustan Times/IMAGO Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps. Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat. His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America. While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online. "There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons." Why target film stars? For Bishnoi, it seems personal. In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community . Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang. Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself." Salman Khan was granted bail in 2018 as he appealed a conviction for killing two rare antelopes Image: AFP But money and intimidation matter too. "Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage. "With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that." Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly." "They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money." Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd." But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW. Is Bollywood under siege? Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave. "I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai. The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added. India's banned film 'Satluj' finds new audiences To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people." At any case, the fear remains real. And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods. "If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah. "Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote. With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign. Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security. Edited by: Darko Janjevic Advertisement

title: Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.
body: Politics Canada Mark Carney: Canada has 'learned we are overdependent on the US' Mark Hallam 10/30/2026 October 30, 2026 Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term "associate membership." https://p.dw.com/p/5Osbl Prefer DW on Google Carney told DW that in 'many cases' there could be scope for deeper Canada-EU cooperation than between Canada and the US Image: Dmytro Rusanov/DW Advertisement Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU . Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump , representing Canada 's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south. "The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said. Canada is too reliant on the United States, Carney tells DW To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did Carney say about EU talks and closer ties to the bloc? An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday. They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor. "Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower. "What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said. Carney and EU leaders met at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal this week Image: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance What scope for EU-Canada cooperation does Carney see? Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner. "We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States." He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges. But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals. Carney said that, like von der Leyen but possibly unlike Germany's Friedrich Merz, he uses the term associate membership to describe the status Canada seeks Image: Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Is Canada concerned the talks could alienate the US, or Trump? Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario , or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents. "The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said. Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues." But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world. Carney has been in the midst of difficult trade talks with Donald Trump, who has at times shown his dissatisfaction with his neighbor to the north as only he can Image: Dmytro Rusanov/DW He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace." Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time." "There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement." Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges. "It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said. Are the EU and Canada moving closer? title: October 30, 2026 - FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Groundbreaking therapy provides additional treatment option that fights the disease at its source, not only its symptoms For Immediate Release: October 30, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), a rare disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that leads to the formation of small, wart-like growths in the patient’s airways. This approval, the first for a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy in the U.S., offers patients a new therapeutic option that targets the root cause of RRP and has been shown to reduce the burden of surgical intervention, representing an important step forward for a patient population with limited treatment options. “Adults living with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often face an exhausting and relentless cycle of repeated surgeries, managing their disease, but never truly escaping it. Today’s approval represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough: a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body’s own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP,” said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) . “For patients, that could mean fewer surgeries, fewer disruptions, and more time living their lives on their own terms. The FDA is proud to help bring that possibility within reach.” The agency based this accelerated approval on clinical trial data showing Voceryq helps reduce the frequency of surgical procedures required to remove growths in adult patients with RRP — an intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The accelerated approval pathway allows the FDA to approve drugs or biologics for serious or life-threatening conditions based on an effect on a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit. RRP is a rare, chronic disease in which wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11 form in the airways, most often around the larynx (voice box), particularly the vocal cords. These growths, called papillomas, can cause symptoms like hoarseness, chronic cough, and voice changes, and in severe cases can spread to other parts of the respiratory tract, causing difficulty breathing. While surgery can remove the growths, there is no cure, and the virus persists in the tissue even after the growths are removed, so patients often need repeated procedures over many years. In some cases, RRP carries a risk of becoming cancerous over time. Voceryq is a recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that delivers two plasmids (small pieces of DNA originally derived from bacteria) into the body’s cells, one of which contains the genetic instructions for specific HPV proteins and the other an immune response-enhancing molecule called IL-12. The therapy is designed to stimulate the immune system to respond to and attack cells infected by the specific types of HPV that cause RRP (types 6 and 11).  Voceryq is administered via intramuscular (IM) injection using the CELLECTRA 5PSP Device, which delivers the dose and facilitates electroporation, a technique which uses brief electrical pulses to temporarily and reversibly create pores in the cell membranes to enable the delivery of Voceryq into the body’s cells. The safety and effectiveness of Voceryq was evaluated in an open-label multicenter clinical trial in 32 adults diagnosed with RRP. Eligible patients had two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the 12 months prior to Voceryq treatment, including a scheduled surgery at trial entry. Seven (27%) out of 26 patients who had at least three baseline surgeries did not require any surgery intervention during the first year after treatment. The most commonly reported adverse reactions to Voceryq were injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension (high blood pressure), nausea, and dizziness. Adverse effects associated with the electroporation technique may include brief muscle contractions or tetany, temporary bleeding at the administration site, anxiety, vasovagal reactions including lightheadedness and dizziness, transient changes in creatine phosphokinase, erythema (skin redness) at the injection site, and pain at the injection site. The FDA granted Voceryq Breakthrough and Orphan Drug designations. The FDA granted accelerated approval of Voceryq to Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA ### Boilerplate The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

title: Report on U.S. Portfolio Holdings of Foreign Securities at Year-End 2025
body: October 30, 2026 Washington – Fial data from an annual survey of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 were released today and posted on the Treasury web site at https://home.treasury.gov/data/treasury-international-capital-tic-system/tic-forms-instructions/us-claims-on-foreigners-from-holdings-of-foreign-securities .  Preliminary data were released and posted on the Treasury web site on August 31, 2025. The survey was undertaken jointly by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. A complementary survey measuring foreign portfolio holdings of U.S. securities also occurs annually.  Data from the most recent such survey, for securities held at end-June 2026, are currently being processed.  Preliminary results are expected to be reported on February 26, 2027. Overall Results This survey measured the value of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 as approximately $19.3 trillion, with $15.2 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.6 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities (original term-to-maturity in excess of one year), and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The previous such survey, conducted as of year-end 2024, measured U.S. holdings of approximately $15.8 trillion, with $12.1 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.3 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities, and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The increase in U.S. holdings of foreign securities in 2025 was mainly in equity (see Table 1). U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities by country at the end of 2025 were the largest for the Cayman Islands ($3.1 trillion), followed by the United Kingdom ($2.0 trillion), Canada ($1.9 trillion), and Japan ($1.5 trillion) (see Table 2). title: ICYMI: Secretary Bessent, Trump Administration Officials Announce New Fraud Prevention Measures in Minnesota
body: October 30, 2026 ST. CLOUD, Minn.— Today, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent traveled to St. Cloud, Minnesota, along with Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Chairman Andrew Ferguson, and Assistant Attorney General for the National Fraud Enforcement Division Colin McDonald, to announce several initiatives to combat the rampant fraud that has wasted billions of taxpayer dollars in Minnesota. Today’s announcements underscore the Trump Administration’s coordinated efforts to protect taxpayer dollars, prevent fraud, and hold perpetrators accountable. Yesterday, FBI Minneapolis executed numerous search warrants related to ongoing fraud investigations in a combined 26- count indictment, and arrested four alleged Medicaid fraudsters who intended to defraud victims of over $41 million with actual losses amounting to $21.65 million . This was the outcome of an investigation by the FBI, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and Homeland Security Investigations. To further strengthen fraud prevention and detection, Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) today issued an alert on risks involving cross-border payments through U.S.-based money services businesses after financial institutions reported more than $8 billion in potentially suspicious wire payments from 2021 to 2025. FinCEN also issued a notice to help financial institutions detect and report the exploitation of charities and nonprofits for terrorist financing, fraud, and other illicit activity. “President Trump has made clear that the war on fraud is not the work of one department, but a mandate we must carry across the Administration,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent . “The U.S. Treasury is deploying every tool to bring an end to this egregious, unchecked fraud and hold perpetrators to account. And under this President’s leadership, wherever the money leads, the full weight of the federal government will follow.” Read Secretary Bessent’s op-ed in the Minnesota Star-Tribune . “Our nation’s War on Fraud began in the Medicaid program right here in Minnesota. Since then, we’ve embarked on an unprecedented quest to crush corruption here and nationwide,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz . “No society, no American, no patient should ever be the victim of the crimes we’ve seen since then. Fraudsters aren’t just stealing taxpayer dollars. they are threatening the quality, affordability, and integrity of the healthcare millions of Americans rely on.” “We’re identifying criminal funding streams, locating their center of gravity, and dismantling their networks across the country. That includes crushing the criminal fraud complex that has plagued America for so long,” said FBI Director Kash Patel . “The FBI is following the money, and if you steal from the government or American taxpayers, justice will find you." “States such as Minnesota got a free pass for four full years. During this time, criminals were allowed to steal money from hardworking Americans and live a life of luxury while everyone else suffered,” said FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson . “President Trump, Vice President Vance, and Secretary Bessent had a very clear message: Enough is enough. The era of robbing American citizens is over. We are putting Americans first again.” “Minnesota is the epicenter for fraud in America,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter for the Justice Department . “The Trump administration’s crackdown is working, and the results speak for themselves. Through the Minnesota Fraud Task Force we are systematically dismantling schemes preying on Americans. Backed by more than a thousand subpoenas and 40 warrants, the message is simple: No one stealing from taxpayer-funded programs is safe.” “The alarming concentration of fraud targeting taxpayer-funded programs in Minnesota demands a coordinated and sustained response,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division . “We are working with our law enforcement partners to uncover alleged fraud, protect public funds, and hold offenders accountable. We will continue these efforts until these schemes are dismantled and taxpayer dollars are protected from abuse in Minnesota.” The full press conference is available to watch here . Read more about Treasury’s announced fraud prevention measures . ###

title: Remarks by Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent on New Fraud Prevention Measures in Minnesota
body: October 30, 2026 As prepared for delivery. ST. CLOUD, Minn .—Good afternoon.  Thank you all for being here today.  I am pleased to be joined by FBI Director Kash Patel, CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, and Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald as we bring new force to the fight against fraud. President Trump has made clear that the war on fraud is not the work of one department, but a mandate we must carry across the Administration.  I am proud to stand alongside so many dedicated colleagues who are delivering on that mandate every day. America is a generous country.  And the compassion of our people imposes a corresponding duty on our government. That is why I visited Minnesota in January to make clear that the U.S. Treasury is deploying every tool to bring an end to this egregious, unchecked fraud and hold perpetrators to account. Over the past year, Treasury returned $175 million in payments that would have gone to deceased individuals—and expanded Do Not Pay access from 4 to 99 percent of federal programs. Further, we’ve stopped almost $190 million and returned over $100 million in funds to U.S. victims of overseas fraud; ordered an audit of approximately $9 billion in Treasury contracts; and, together with our partners at the IRS, proposed stronger eligibility checks for health insurance tax credits. These actions form one front of a whole-of-government effort led by Vice President Vance.  The Vice President’s task force first convened in March.  And he has worked tirelessly to restore vigilance and responsible stewardship in the management of public money. Since January 2025, the Trump Administration has uncovered more than $260 billion in fraud, prevented $72 billion in taxpayer funds from going out the door to illicit actors annually, and brought enforcement actions involving nearly $60 billion. Nowhere is this work more urgent than here in Minnesota. In the weeks following my visit, Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, known as FinCEN, issued a Geographic Targeting Order to trace criminal networks that divert funds overseas—and ensure that taxpayer dollars go to the American people, not terror groups like al-Shabaab.  We have ongoing investigations at home and abroad into al-Shabaab, its network and its enablers. Since the start of the Trump Administration, FinCEN data have also supported the law enforcement effort that led to the arrest and charging of 115 fraudsters, as well as seventy-five convictions and nearly 3,000 subpoenas across Minnesota. And just yesterday, IRS-CI assisted with investigative activity at several sites suspected of fraud.  I want to give a shoutout to our great officers at IRS-CI.  They don’t get much press, but they are quietly one of the most effective groups in the United States government for fighting fraud. Today, FinCEN released additional information to help refer new leads to law enforcement and provide support to ongoing investigations. We issued a notice to help financial institutions identify and report suspicious activity, especially involving charities and nonprofits. The notice highlights how criminals exploit fundraising capabilities to facilitate terrorist financing, fraud, and other illicit activity. FinCEN also issued an alert on the risks associated with cross-border transactions originated by money services businesses, known as MSBs. The alert details how bad actors can exploit MSBs to move funds overseas. FinCEN identified over $8 billion in potentially suspicious foreign agent-directed payments between 2021 and 2025 alone. And today’s alert urges financial institutions to be vigilant in detecting, identifying, and reporting suspicious activity arising from certain cross-border payments involving U.S.-based MSBs. The next phase of this fight, meanwhile, will make it easier than ever for whistleblowers who know where fraud is hiding to lead us to it. Until now, any citizen who detected fraud was forced to navigate a maze of tip lines scattered across law enforcement agencies. No more. For the first time, we’ve created a single, centralized portal at America.gov/fraud. Treasury is proud to seed this new, $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program. And anyone who submits information that leads to a conviction or enforcement action may be eligible for a reward up to $30,000. Speaking up has long carried a cost for whistleblowers. Under President Trump, it can offer a reward. Now, the industrial-scale fraud that Tim Walz shamefully, and perhaps knowingly, allowed to fester is the defining legacy of his administration. But with President Trump back in office, Washington is no longer content to watch Minnesota’s fraud epidemic spiral from a distance. The days of indifference are over. And under this President’s leadership, wherever the money leads, the full weight of government will follow. Now, I am pleased to turn it over to someone who has helped to give the fight against fraud both its discipline and its force, FBI Director Kash Patel. ###

title: Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya
body: Politics Libya Smuggling, power, profit: Irregular migration out of eastern Libya Kersten Knipp 10/30/2026 October 30, 2026 There is currently more irregular migration between eastern Libya and Crete, Greece. It's raising questions as to what connects people smugglers with powerful militias in eastern Libya and then in turn, Europeans. https://p.dw.com/p/5Orv4 Prefer DW on Google A rescue of refugees in distress off the Libyan coast Image: Laurin Schmid/SOS MEDITERRANEE/picture alliance Advertisement This year, almost 20,000 people have already tried to make the perilous crossing from Libya in north Africa to the Greek island of Crete. The route, which runs from the east coast of Libya to Greece, has become an increasingly significant corridor for irregular migration into Europe, Greek daily Kathimerini recently reported. On Oct. 20 alone, Greek authorities registered 710 people in 14 boats . Hundreds more arrived the next day. Many of the boats depart from areas around Tobruk, a port city on Libya's eastern Mediterranean coast. According to Kathimerini, migrants pay as much as $4,000 (€3,600) for the crossing, which takes around a day and a half. This particular route is becoming more popular in part because of crackdowns on alternative passages. After eastern Libyan armed forces acted against people smugglers heading for Italy in 2023, the smuggling networks changed their methods, using smaller boats and sailing them towards Crete instead. Libyans protest against irregular migration in front of the International Organization for Migration office in Tripoli, June 2026 Image: Mahmud Turkia/AFP Fuelling the conflict economy According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a think tank based in Switzerland, other groups have since entered the people smuggling business too, including those who previously mostly moved goods, vehicles or drugs. Human trafficking in Libya is closely connected with what is known as  the "conflict economy." This sees armed actors gaining economic resources and political influence by controlling informal markets and transport routes. It also sees local power brokers using measures against smuggling to obtain financial or political support for themselves. Social media's hidden role in human trafficking, smuggling To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Conflict and subsequent instability in Libya have created a fertile environment for migrant smuggling and TIP [trafficking in persons] activities to develop, in turn leading to the growth of smuggling in other locations along an established route," researchers at British think tank Chatham House wrote, after looking in depth at three different transit hubs across Libya. "This has led to an increase in the number of migrants entering Libya and the expansion of Libya's conflict economy." "It remains the case that an entire business has developed around smuggling routes, regardless of whether that [smuggling] involves weapons, goods, people or drugs," Hager Ali, a researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, told DW. If there are already contacts, transportation and security arrangements in place, then these can also be used for illegal activities like people trafficking, Ali said. Since 2014, Libya has been split into two . In the west, a United Nations-backed administration is based in Tripol; and in the east, in Tobruk, the second Libyan leadership is backed by former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar. Haftar has managed to consolidate control over various armed militias, ruling with an iron fist. His sons also hold important positions. However, there are no proven links between the Haftars' networks and people smugglers on that coast. But, as Ali explained, even the appearance of having some influence over these sectors can confer political influence. "The more apparent control one has over this market, the greater one's influence," Ali told DW. A powerful and controversial figure in eastern Libya: Khalifa Haftar Image: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images Those Libyans who can influence, or even prevent, departures are demonstrating their importance to other actors. For example, high profile operations against the smuggling networks can serve as a sign of political legitimacy. "They present themselves as somebody who can restore order and curb migration," Ali noted. There's also increasing geopolitical competition in the eastern Mediterranean. In late October, the Tobruk government signed a maritime agreement with Turkey , a deal that Turkey had actually originally concluded with Libya's other government in Tripoli. Turkey previously fought Haftar-sponsored militias during the Libyan civil war, and this deal represents rapprochement between the two. It is also a way for Turkey to get what it wants in a rivalrous situation in this maritime area — Greece rejects the agreement, saying that it infringes on Greek economic rights around islands like Crete and Rhodes. A direct link between the new agreement and rising numbers of irregular migrants in Crete is not clear. However, Ali suggested that it wouldn't be inconceivable that irregular migrants could be used as leverage in these kinds of geopolitical conflicts. European cooperation The European Union has been cooperating with Libyans to prevent irregular migrants from getting to Europe — despite the Libyan actors' links to armed groups and their disputed political legitimacy. There's an obvious contradiction in that, argued Andreas Dittmann, a retired professor from Giessen University and expert on human geography and development. Such cooperation between the EU and Libyans can serve as a control on irregular migration but it also adds to the Libyans' local power. "If those in charge in eastern Libya are actually able to influence the scale and timing of such [migrant] movements, they're demonstrating their own strategic importance to European governments," Dittmann told DW. A report by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, or IOM, illustrated how precarious the situation is for many migrants. According to the report, which is based on data from May and June this year, around 950,000 migrants and refugees were registered as living in Libya. Many have only limited access to healthcare and tend not to have residence or work permits, all of which increases their dependence on informal markets as well as the risk of exploitation . This story was originally published in German. Advertisement

title: Secretary Bessent, Senior U.S. Officials Announce New Fraud Prevention Measures in Minnesota
body: October 30, 2026 Initiatives Aim to Stop Unchecked Fraud, Strengthen Accountability, and Restore Integrity to the State ST. CLOUD, Minn. —In Minnesota, alongside other senior U.S. officials, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent today announced several initiatives to combat the rampant fraud that has wasted billions of dollars in Minnesota. As part of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, Treasury continues to work tirelessly to protect American taxpayer dollars and restore integrity to federal benefits programs. “When greed meets negligence, the American people suffer,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent . “Under President Trump and Vice President Vance’s leadership, Treasury stopped nearly $190 million in funds tied to overseas fraud and returned more than $100 million to U.S. victims. We are working with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud to help prevent this kind of abuse from happening again, in Minnesota or anywhere else.” Secretary Bessent visited the Twin Cities earlier this year to announce several Treasury initiatives and investigations aimed at combating fraud in Minnesota. He met with representatives from financial institutions, fraud victims, state leaders, and affected community members. During that trip, Treasury also held training sessions for state and local law enforcement on detecting and investigating fraud. Treasury has continued to support federal, state, and local law enforcement with data that is essential to generating new leads, investigating fraud, and dismantling fraud schemes. IRS-CI BRINGS ACCOUNTABILITY TO MINNESOTA This week, Salim Said, co-conspirator in the Feeding Our Future fraud scheme that exploited a federally funded child nutrition program during the COVID-19 pandemic, was sentenced to 30 years in federal prison. These cases result from an investigation conducted by the FBI, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and Homeland Security Investigations. Said was the owner of Safari Restaurant, which was utilized as an alleged food distribution site. As determined at trial, Said participated in a scheme to defraud the Federal Child Nutrition Program under the sponsorship of Feeding Our Future of $49 million. Said was convicted at trial on 21 counts related to wire fraud, money laundering, bribery and conspiracy. FINCEN ALERTS FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS TO RISKS OF CERTAIN CROSS-BORDER PAYMENTS INVOLVING MSBs From 2021 to 2025, U.S. financial institutions reported more than $8 billion in potentially suspicious wire payments sent through U.S.-based money services businesses (MSBs) at the direction of foreign agents, which help facilitate transnational transactions. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) today issued an alert asking financial institutions to watch for suspicious activity involving certain cross-border payments involving U.S. MSBs. Bad actors may exploit certain U.S. MSBs’ cross-border relationships to move funds through the U.S. financial system while obscuring the ultimate beneficiaries and the underlying purposes of transactions. These structures can help conceal illicit activity, such as funding for terrorist organizations. FINCEN ISSUES NOTICE TO STOP ILLICIT ACTIVITY EXPLOITING CHARITIES AND NON-PROFITS FinCEN today also issued a notice to help financial institutions detect and report suspicious activity involving the exploitation of charities and non-profit organizations. Fraudsters sometimes exploit the fundraising capabilities of charities and non-profit organizations to facilitate terrorist financing, fraud, and other illicit activity. Bad actors may funnel funds to terrorists, divert taxpayer dollars from government programs, and steal money intended for charitable causes. The notice describes three types of schemes exploiting charities and non-profit organizations: sham charities, which involve bad actors falsely advertising a legitimate purpose for a charity or non-profit organization but using funds for illicit activity (including terrorism); fraud schemes, which involve bad actors falsely advertising a legitimate purpose for a charity or non-profit organization but using funds to support their lifestyle; and embezzlement, which involves insiders abusing their position of trust at a legitimate charity or non-profit organization to steal money. MATERIALS Alert on Risks Associated with Foreign-Agent-Directed Transactions Notice on the Use of Charities and Non-Profit Organizations for Illicit Activity

title: We’ve received our first response from the Project Suncatcher prototype satellite.
body: We’ve received our first response from the Project Suncatcher prototype satellite. Travis Beals Senior Director, Paradigms of Intelligence Oct 30, 2026 On October 1, we launched our prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher. The launch marked the first step in our long-term research moonshot to explore powering AI compute in space. Since then, we've spent the last few weeks completing our commissioning checklist, which included powering up the host and TPU trays and successfully running early machine learning tests. This week, we reached our "Hello World" milestone: the first-ever AI response from a data center class TPU in orbit. During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space. As the satellite passed by Svalbard, Norway, the downlinked poem confirmed success: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Following this initial output, we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems. Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit. Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027. Our chips have officially earned their space wings — an important achievement on the long road ahead for this cosmic moonshot.

title: Philip R. Lane: AI adoption in Europe
body:
AI adoption in Europe Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Philip R. Lane Member of the ECB's Executive Board SPEECH AI adoption in Europe Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy San Francisco, 30 October 2026 My aim today is to describe how AI is reshaping the euro area economy. [ 1 ] Although the development of frontier AI models is primarily taking place in the United States and China, the adoption of AI will be a key determinant of European productivity growth in the coming years, while expenditure on AI adoption also currently constitutes a significant stimulus to the euro area economy. [ 2 ] In addition, European firms are part of the global AI supply chain, while European investors are contributing to the funding of the global buildout of AI infrastructure through equity and debt markets and the banking system. I will also describe the key patterns we see in the data, with a primary focus on how the surveys conducted by the ECB can provide insights into the AI adoption process and the implications for the financial system. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] Aggregate trends Digital investment in the euro area has expanded by 73 per cent in real terms since 2014, increasing from 2.3 per cent to 3.3 per cent of GDP (Chart 1a). While digital investment has grown far more quickly in the United States, the surge in digital investment (with an estimated clear acceleration since 2024) marks a distinct shift in the structure of the euro area economy. [ 5 ] As shown in Chart 1b, in the euro area digital investment has primarily been in intangible assets, while investment in data centres has constituted a relatively small share. [ 6 ] Chart 1 Digital investment in the euro area a) Digital investment proxy, euro area b) Digital investment proxy, euro area, with asset breakdown (2014 = 100) (EUR billion) Sources: Eurostat, ECB and ECB calculations. Notes: Chart 1a shows the digital proxy for the euro area business economy, at constant 2020 prices, indexed to 2014. The blue dots for 2025 and 2026 extend the digital investment proxy based on the annual growth of an output proxy for digital services (weighted non-seasonally adjusted production of publishing activities; computer programming, consultancy and related activities; and information service activities). Chart 1b shows a digital proxy which refers to (i) investment in non-residential buildings and structures in the information and communication sector, (ii) information and communication technology (ICT) equipment in the business economy, (iii) investment in computer software and databases (CSDBs) in the business economy, excluding the ICT sector, and (iv) total intellectual property products (IPP) investment (in CSDBs and research and development) by the ICT sector. Missing country values are estimated based on known euro area aggregates of country-sector shares. On a whole-economy basis, digital investment has increased from around 2.3 per cent of euro area GDP in 2014 to 3.0 per cent in 2024 (and looks to have increased to 3.3 per cent by the end of the first half of 2026, on the basis of updates of digital services output). The latest observations are for 2024 for euro area annual accounts and July 2026 for euro area production data. In the ECB Corporate Telephone Survey, firms report that AI has added about 10 per cent to their capital expenditure plans this year. AI-related demand has helped activity to hold up over the last two years – as reflected by the contributions of the “computers and other electronics” and “information and communication services” sectors to total market production (Chart 2a). As illustrated in Chart 2b, Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) indicators show that output, employment and new orders have developed considerably more favourably in the technology equipment subsector than in other manufacturing subsectors. For services, the software subsector has performed better than other services sectors in terms of output, albeit not in terms of employment and new orders. Chart 2 Effects of the global AI boom on euro area output a) Total market production b) PMIs for technology equipment and software in manufacturing and services (cumulated changes since January 2025 in per cent) (diffusion indices, average January-September 2026) Sources: Eurostat and ECB calculations Note: The latest observations are for July 2026. Sources: S&P Global and ECB calculations. Notes: Sectoral labels are taken from the July Global PMI press release. The latest observations are for September 2026. AI has been the main driver of global goods trade over the last year (Chart 3a). European firms are contributors to the global AI supply chain. Table 4 shows that AI-related exports and imports are growing quickly in the euro area, especially in relation to core data centre goods, which contain directly deployed hardware components related to AI compute, storage and networking capacity. Possibly related to differences in composition, the increase in AI import prices in the euro area is more muted than for the other major economic regions (Chart 3b). Chart 5 shows that, while AI-related price increases have contributed materially to the upward shift in goods inflation, the impact on headline inflation is limited owing to the relatively low weight of AI-exposed goods in the consumer price index (13.3 per cent in the non-energy industrial goods subcomponent and 3.4 per cent of the HICP). Chart 3 Trade in goods and import prices of AI goods a) Global goods imports by category b) Import prices of AI goods (annual percentage changes, percentage points; de-meaned) (annual percentage changes, three-month moving averages) Sources: Trade Data Monitor and ECB staff calculations. Notes: The figures are nominal data. Values are deviations from their respective mean over 2019-2023. “AI-related” reflects a basket of goods related to the construction and operation of AI data centres estimated by Emter et al. (2026) following Waugh (2026). The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Sources: Trade Data Monitor, ECB and ECB staff calculations. Notes: Import prices are calculated as unit values. “AI goods” is a basket of goods related to AI data centre construction (Emter et al. 2026; Waugh 2026). Unless otherwise indicated, prices are in US dollars. “Asia – AI exporters” includes Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the Philippines. The latest observations are for July 2026 for the euro area, Asia and Global, August 2026 for the United States and September 2026 for China. Table 4 Trade in AI goods Trade in AI-related goods and subcomponents (percentage of total trade; annual growth, percentage) Sources: Eurostat, Trade Data Monitor and ECB staff calculations. Notes: The table shows the share and growth in values. Rest of the world refers to the world excluding the euro area and the United States. 2023 shares are the shares of imports/exports in total imports/exports of the respective country or region. “AI-related trade” refers to goods related to the construction and operation of AI data centres (Emter et al., 2026; Waugh, 2026). “Core data centre goods” are directly deployed hardware components related to AI compute, storage, and networking capacity. “Data centre infrastructure goods” are physical infrastructure goods required to power, cool, and operate data centre facilities. “Other AI-related goods” are upstream AI goods and broad industrial goods used in AI production. Chart 5 Price pressures from rising prices for AI goods a) Consumer product exposure to AI goods b) HICP weights of AI-exposed goods (percentage of output) (percentage points) Sources: Trade Data Monitor, BEA (US Bureau of Economic Analysis), Eurostat and ECB staff calculations. Notes: “AI goods” is a basket of goods related to AI data centre construction (Emter et al. 2026; Waugh, 2026). The data are based on US BEA tables (2017). Exposures are weighted by AI share, based on 2025 nominal trade data. Sources: Eurostat and ECB staff calculations. Note: HICP weights in 2026. In relation to trade in services, Chart 6 shows a significant upward movement in software licence imports from the United States since 2022, consistent with increased purchasing of AI licences from the leading US firms. [ 7 ] Chart 6 Euro area intellectual property products imports Euro area payments for the use of intellectual property products (imports) (four-quarter moving sums in EUR billions) Sources: ECB (euro area balance of payments), BEA (US Bureau of Economic Analysis, US trade in services) and ECB staff calculations. Notes: Euro area charges for the use of intellectual property (imports) are based on quarterly ECB balance of payments data. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Imports from the United States are broken down by type of intellectual property using annual shares by type in US exports to the euro area, as reported by the BEA (mirror data). These shares are applied to quarterly euro area imports of intellectual property from the United States for the corresponding year. The latest available BEA data refer to 2025; the 2025 shares are also applied to 2026 quarters. European investors are also major purchasers of US technology-related equities (Chart 7). Listed European tech firms have also benefited from rising stock market valuations (Chart 8a). Stock returns, revenue growth, operating margin growth and earnings per share growth are all increasing in AI-intensity (Chart 8b). Chart 7 Euro area purchases of US shares Net purchases of listed US corporate shares by euro area residents (cumulated flows in EUR billions) Sources: ECB SHSS (Securities Holdings Statistics by Sector), LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) Data & Analytics, ECB calculations. Notes: The sectoral breakdown is obtained using information from LSEG Data & Analytics on the firms issuing the shares whose International Securities Identification Number (ISIN) is identified in SHSS data. “Other sectors” includes academic and educational services, basic materials, financials, healthcare, institutions, associations and organisations, real estate, energy, industrials, utilities and consumer. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Chart 8 Performance of European AI-related stocks since January 2023 a) Performance of European stock market indices since January 2023 b) Stock performance and financial metrics of Euro Stoxx 600 firms by AI intensity since January 2023 (percentages) (lower right panel: EUR; other panels: percentage points) Sources: Bloomberg, LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) and ECB calculations. Notes: Chart 8a shows stock market returns since 2 January 2023, in percentages in euro after adjusting for exchange rate movements, of the S&P500 and Euro Stoxx 600 indices, the subindices S&P 500 Information and Technology excluding Magnificent 7, Magnificent 7 and Euro Stoxx 600 Technology. Magnificent 7 firms comprise: Alphabet (Google), Amazon, Apple, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Tesla. Chart 8b shows stock market returns since 2 January 2023 in percentage points of value-weighted portfolios of Euro Stoxx 600 firms sorted by their AI classification. AI intensity groups are based on OECD methodology (for details, see “ A sectoral taxonomy of AI intensity ”, OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers , No 30, December 2024). The classification comprises three AI intensity groups: high, medium and low, based on sectoral quartile allocations across four indicators: 1. AI human capital; 2. AI innovation; 3. Barrier-adjusted AI exposure; and 4. AI use. A sector is classified as high if it ranks in the top quartile for at least two indicators and not in the bottom quartile for the remaining two, and as low if it ranks in the bottom quartile for at least two indicators and not in the top quartile for the remaining two. Sectors such as IT services, media, telecommunications, finance and scientific research and development are classified as high-intensity, while food products, textiles, wood and paper, construction and hospitality are low-intensity. Sectors falling outside these criteria are classified as medium AI-intensive. The latest observations are for 20 October 2026. US firms (especially the hyperscalers building out the AI infrastructure) have been large-scale issuers of euro-denominated bonds (reverse Yankees). So far, the available data show that purchases by European investors of euro-denominated bonds issued by US firms have increased alongside a decline in their purchases of US Treasury bonds (Chart 9a). [ 8 ] The AI boom has also led to large initial public offerings (IPOs), including the SpaceX IPO in the second quarter of 2026. In this context, euro area investors have stepped up their acquisitions of US equities, and at the same time they have lowered their purchases of other foreign equities (Chart 9b). Overall, these developments, together with analysis of credit spreads and the book-cover ratios of euro area corporate issuers and credit spreads, suggest only limited crowding-out up to now. [ 9 ] Chart 9 Absorption of US AI issuance in the euro area a) Issuance and absorption of reverse Yankees b) US IPOs and euro area purchases of foreign equities (average of quarterly flows in EUR billions) (average of quarterly flows in EUR billions) Source: ECB SHSS (Securities Holdings Statistics by Sector). Notes: Reverse Yankees refer to euro-denominated bonds issued by US firms. Euro area purchases refer to the non-MFI sector. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Sources: ECB SHSS (Securities Holdings Statistics by Sector)and Dealogic. Notes: Euro area purchases refer to the non-MFI sector. “RoW” stands for rest of the world. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Finally, lending to AI-related firms has contributed substantially to aggregate credit growth. This is evident in Chart 10, which shows that the ECB Broad Intermediate Gauge (ECB-BIG) index would have indicated a tighter credit environment in the absence of AI-related lending. In response to a dedicated question in the October 2026 bank lending survey on the significance and impact of AI adoption, several banks indicated that they expect a gradual but sustained increase in loan demand to finance digital infrastructure, particularly data centres. Banks also reported that their current and prospective AI-related lending is more likely to target infrastructure providers rather than software developers or firms adopting AI, with this focus expected to become more pronounced over the coming months. Chart 10 Effect of AI on intermediation conditions ECB-BIG index (index – higher means tighter intermediation conditions) Sources: NL Analytics, PATSTAT (Patent Statistical Database), ECB, ECB projections database, Allayioti, Di Casola and Magistretti (2026) and ECB calculations. Notes: The ECB Broad Intermediation Gauge (ECB-BIG) index uses a BVAR model with mixed-frequency. Price components include lending rates and the FCI; Quantity components include credit volumes and data from the bank lending survey. Shaded areas represent the 90 per cent confidence bands. The counterfactual assumes that the share of AI patents after June 2024 remained constant, conditioning only on the AI news shock. The latest observations are for October 2026. I will now turn from aggregate trends to firm-level and household-level surveys on AI adoption before examining how AI is being funded by the financial system. AI adoption The pace of AI adoption by European firms has trended upwards since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. Chart 11 shows that the proportion of firms citing AI-related topics in earnings calls has expanded from about 10 per cent to about 40 per cent over this period. A similar pattern is evident in our Corporate Telephone Survey. Chart 11 Alternative measures of AI adoption Proportion of firms mentioning AI or related terms (percentage of firms) Sources: NL Analytics, Corporate Telephone Survey Team and ECB calculations. Notes: CTS (Corporate Telephone Survey) refers to the proportion of euro area firms which mentioned “AI” during the call; Earnings calls refer to the quarterly average proportion of euro area firms which mentioned “AI”, “artificial intelligence”, “machine learning”, “large language models”, “LLM”, or alternatives during the earnings call. The dashed lines indicate the trend since the second quarter of 2023. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. The earnings calls data show significant variation across sectors. [ 10 ] The left panel of Chart 12 shows that there has been an increase in the range of sectors in which firms frame AI as an innovation that expands the technology frontier. Although less widespread, there has also been an increase in the range of sectors in which AI is seen as potentially reducing costs by improving production efficiency (right panel). Chart 12 AI adoption across the European economy Share of Euro STOXX 600 AI-exposed companies by adoption type (percentages) Sources: LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) and ECB calculations. Notes: The sample covers all Euro STOXX 600 constituents from the first quarter of 2017 to the second quarter of 2026. The chart shows, for each Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) sector, the annual share of firms whose earnings calls mention AI in connection with innovation and growth (left panel) or productivity and efficiency (right panel), according to the classification introduced in Ferrari, I., Groß, J., Schupp, F. and Steffensen, S. (2026), “AI Exposure and the Costs of Market-based Financing in Europe: Evidence from Earnings Call Transcripts”, mimeo. Figures for 2026 are based on the first two quarters of the year. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. While the earnings calls data cover publicly listed firms, our Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) is a large-scale survey that covers both large firms and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). [ 11 ] In the fourth quarter of 2025 most firms participating in the SAFE reported that they were using AI: 64 per cent of firms said they were using it either experimentally or moderately, while only 7 per cent of firms reported that their use was “significant” (Chart 13). [ 12 ] In terms of the reasons to use AI, 62 per cent cited improving business processes and 23 per cent cited innovation, research and development or expanding their range of products, while just 15 per cent cited reducing labour costs. Chart 13 AI use and reasons for adopting or not adopting AI in the euro area a) Use of AI by firm size b) Reasons for using AI (percentages of respondents) (percentages of respondents) Sources: ECB SAFE (Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises) and ECB calculations. Notes: Chart 13a shows the weighted share of firms by the intensity of AI use, for all firms, by size class. Chart 13b shows the weighted share of firms by reasons for using AI. For the chart 13b, the base is firms which use AI very infrequently, moderately or significantly. The latest observations are for the fourth quarter of 2025. The round of the SAFE survey conducted in the fourth quarter of 2025 also ran a field experiment to test whether planned AI investment by a firm responds to perceived competitive pressure from domestic peer firms and foreign peer firms. [ 13 ] Chart 14a shows that firms underestimate the rate of AI adoption by their peer firms, with most firms underestimating the share of competitors that have invested in AI, some by as much as 50 percentage points. The results of the field experiment indicate that providing information about the AI investment plans of their peers makes firms change their beliefs. In the field experiment, half of the firms were randomly told the true share of peers investing in AI, at home and abroad. These firms revised up their beliefs about the share of peers investing in AI, by 4.3 percentage points for domestic competitors and 3.3 percentage points for foreign competitors. Chart 14b shows a striking asymmetry: firms plan more AI investment when they expect more domestic peers to invest, whereas beliefs about the AI investment plans of foreign firms have no effect. The impact of domestic competition is sizeable: a 1 percentage point increase in the expected share of domestic firms undertaking AI investment raises their own expected AI investment rate by about 0.6 percentage points. That is a marked increase, given an average expected AI investment rate of 8.3 per cent. Chart 14 Perception of firms’ AI adoption and effects of competition on investment a) Misperception about AI adoption by competitors b) Impact of competition on own future AI investment (percentage points) (left panel: percentages; right panel: percentage points) Source: Baumann et al. (2026) . Notes: The chart shows the distribution of the difference between the actual share of firms investing in AI and firms’ perceived adoption rates by domestic and foreign competitors up to June 2025 as indicated by firms, before receiving information on the true share of competitor firms investing in AI. A positive difference between the true share of firms investing and firms’ prior beliefs indicates underestimation. The latest observations are for December 2025. Source: Baumann et al. (2026) . Notes: The left panel shows how firms update their beliefs about the share of domestic and foreign competitors investing in AI over the next twelve months, after receiving information on the true share of domestic/foreign competitors which invested in AI until June 2025. The right panel shows the impact of domestic and foreign competition on firms’ own expected AI investment rate. The dependent variable is firm-level expected AI investment as a share of total investment, taking a value between 0 and 100. The latest observations are for December 2025. According to the round of the SAFE survey conducted in the second quarter of 2026, among firms planning AI-related investment over the next twelve months, most expect to invest in AI-related technologies and tools, as well as in employee training. Firms were allowed to indicate multiple types of expected AI-related investment: 49 per cent plan to invest in AI technologies and tools (e.g. software licences), 46 per cent in training employees, 40 per cent in data and infrastructure, and 12 per cent in hiring AI specialists. Investment patterns are broadly similar across firm sizes, although the shares are consistently higher for large firms than for SMEs across all investment types. Chart 15 Types of expected AI investment Types of expected AI investment, by firm size (percentages of respondents) Sources: ECB SAFE (Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises) and ECB calculations. Notes: The chart shows the weighted share of firms by the type of expected AI investment over the next 12 months, for all firms and by size class. The latest observations are for June 2026. Turning to AI adoption by workers, our Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) asks households on a regular basis about AI usage in the workplace. According to the CES, the proportion of workers using AI has doubled over the last two years, with 52 per cent now reporting that they use AI at work, compared with 26 per cent in 2024 (Chart 16a). [ 14 ] Adoption rates are higher for younger and more educated workers (Chart 16b). [ 15 ] Chart 16 AI adoption rates in the euro area a) AI adoption rates among workers, 2024-2026 b) AI adoption rates by demographic groups, 2026 (percentage of respondents) (percentage of respondents) Sources: CES (Consumer Expectations Survey) and ECB calculations based on the earning calls database. Notes: The chart shows the share of employed workers reporting the use of AI in their work. The question reads: “Do you personally use artificial intelligence (including a large language model, such as ChatGPT or Gemini) in your work?” Chart 17a reports the time saved by workers on a range of tasks. The median working user reports saving three hours per week, or about 7.7 per cent of median working time. [ 16 ] However, the distribution is highly skewed: most users enjoy only moderate time savings, while a small number report very high efficiency gains. Generating or debugging code yields the largest gains, at six hours per week, although only around 15 per cent of workers use AI for this purpose. A similar pattern emerges for data analysis, automation of routine tasks and creating audio or visual content. By contrast, research, information gathering, writing and text editing are among the most frequently cited uses. Yet time savings reported for these tasks are considerably lower than for more technical tasks such as coding. In most professions, workers do not see perceived efficiency gains as a threat to their jobs (Chart 17b). The occupations that have the highest adoption rates tend to save the most hours and have more positive views of AI. For example, managers use AI the most, save the most time and ultimately have the most positive perception of the technology; this places them in a good position to help steer AI adoption in the workplace. [ 17 ] Chart 17 AI at the workplace and hours saved a) Tasks performed with AI and hours saved per week b) Hours saved, adoption and sentiment about AI across occupations (upper scale: percentage of workers using AI; lower scale: median number of hours per week) (x-axis: percentage of workers; y-axis: number of hours saved per week) Source: Dias da Silva, A., Lebastard, L. and Sondermann D. (2026), “ AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report ”, The ECB Blog , ECB, 26 August. Notes: The chart combines two survey questions: (i) “In a typical week last month, how many additional hours do you think you would have needed to complete the same amount of work without using artificial intelligence (AI)?” and (ii) “For which of the following tasks do you typically use artificial intelligence (AI) in your work?”. Time saved per task represents the average total weekly hours saved by workers who reported using AI for that specific activity. Respondents can select multiple tasks, and those who reported saving significant time with AI are more likely to choose a greater number of tasks, which mechanically inflates the average hours saved. Source: Dias da Silva, A., Lebastard, L. and Sondermann D. (2026), “ AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report ”, The ECB Blog , ECB, 26 August. Notes: Dot colours represent net sentiment about the impact of AI on jobs, with red representing net negative sentiment and shades of blue indicating a scale of positive sentiment, with the highest net positive being dark blue. The chart contains information about three survey questions, (i) “In a typical week last month, how many additional hours do you think you would have needed to complete the same amount of work without using artificial intelligence (AI)?”, (ii) “Do you personally use artificial intelligence (AI) in your work (including tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.)?” and (iii) “Do you think that technological advancements (e.g. the increasing use of artificial intelligence, large language models, automation) will affect your current job or employment prospects in the next five years?”. Chart 18a shows that employment perceptions are net positive for all education levels and all demographic groups, with the most positive beliefs among the younger, more educated workers. Chart 18b shows that employment perceptions are net positive for all economic sectors but that the share reporting negative perceptions is highest for professional services and financial services. Notes: 2026 data. The question reads “Do you think that technological advancements (e.g. the increasing use of artificial intelligence, large language models, automation) will affect your current job or employment prospects in the next five years?” with three possible answers: a) Yes, they will affect me positively (e.g. by increasing my productivity and/or improving my employment prospects); b) Yes, they will affect me negatively (e.g. by making my job less necessary and/ or worsening my employment prospects); and c) No, they will not affect me at all. The perceptions shown in Chart 18b exclude workers who expect no effect of technological advancements (such as AI or automation) on their current or future employment prospects. Perceptions are reported for all workers independently of their AI usage. This sectoral ranking is broadly consistent with task-based calculations of occupational AI exposures (Chart 19a). [ 18 ] To illustrate the possible economic impact of a global increase in productivity in the IT sector (where the time savings from AI are greatest), Chart 19b reports a model-based simulation of a 30 per cent increase in productivity. [ 19 ] Chart 19 shows the euro area in 2030, five years after the shock. The overall result is that a productivity gain concentrated in one small industry lifts real wages across the economy, but the jobs lost are concentrated in that industry and among the workers whose tasks it replaces. The IT sector shows 4.4 per cent fewer jobs but a 4.3 per cent increase in real wages. In the model, the rise in sectoral productivity triggers a relative price decline of about one third, with relative demand rising by 28 per cent. Employment of clerical workers outside the IT sector also declines (0.9 per cent fewer jobs) but their real wages increase (3.2 per cent). For managers, professional and technicians outside the IT sector, there is no change in employment and a 4.4 per cent increase in real wages. These workers are complements to IT inputs (elasticities 0 to 0.5): cheaper IT raises what they can do rather than replaces them. Finally, manual and service workers see no change in jobs while their real wages rise by 5.4 per cent. These workers are not directly affected by IT; they gain through higher demand and lower prices. The headline macroeconomic picture is an increase of 3.8 per cent in euro-area output by 2030 (4.1 per cent in the long run) and a 5.5 per cent increase in consumption in the long run. In terms of barriers to AI adoption by workers, one-third of respondents explain that they do not use AI because it is irrelevant for their current tasks (Chart 20a). Other respondents prefer traditional methods or are discouraged by accuracy and reliability concerns, or a lack of provision from their employer. More broadly, Chart 20b shows that a substantial share of workers simply expresses no appetite for the technology: 41 per cent are uninterested in using AI (34 per cent of managers). When asked what would encourage them to adopt AI, around half of all workers point to better training on using AI tools and a better understanding of the usefulness of AI. Employers appear to be responding to some of these needs. About half of firms plan to invest in AI training over the next 12 months (according to the latest SAFE survey wave), directly addressing the barrier most frequently cited by workers. Conversely, this means that around half of firms are not investing in AI training – this is possibly also affected by one-third of managers not being interested enough in AI. A comparison of the AI financing plans of firms within the same country, industry and size class indicates that more tangible investment tilts financing towards external sources (Chart 23). The use of external finance for AI appears to hinge on the tangibility of the underlying investment: assets that are pledgeable or collateralisable attract external funding, whereas more intangible expenditures are financed internally. Investments in hardware and data infrastructure typically require large upfront capital outlays that exceed available internal cash flow while providing pledgeable collateral, prompting firms to seek complementary external funding. In contrast, employee training represents a smaller, more incremental and intangible expense that firms can more readily finance out of retained earnings. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of collateral in securing external financing. This pattern may also point to a potential financing gap for intangible investments, which are critical for building long-term AI capabilities.
