Firms that prioritise internal funds for AI may need external financing for other operational needs. To explore these dynamics, Chart 24 examines the financing choices of firms since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, comparing them with the preceding period. Chart 24a shows that firms in high AI-exposed sectors tend to rely more on internal funds and credit lines than firms in low-AI exposed sectors, although the differences are not very large: 32 per cent of firms in high-AI exposure sectors reported having used internal funds and 22 per cent credit lines, compared with 29 per cent and 19 per cent of those in low-AI exposure sectors. The result for credit lines aligns with recent findings from the United States where banks play a key role in facilitating AI adoption by providing liquidity through credit lines. [ 23 ] High AI-exposed firms also report having issued more equities and debt securities, even if these market-based instruments are not widely used overall among firms in the SAFE sample. Bank loans remain a common source of external finance (19 per cent of firms), with no significant differences across sectors based on AI exposure. Since late 2022, firms in high AI-exposure sectors have shown a relative increase in their use of credit lines, bank loans and debt securities compared with those in low AI-exposure sectors (Chart 24b). Compared with the period before late 2022, the share of firms in high AI-exposed sectors using bank loans rose by 1.8 percentage points more than that of firms in low AI-exposed sectors. The corresponding relative increases are 1.7 percentage points for credit lines and 0.5 percentage points for debt securities. Among SMEs, there is also a rise in the reported use of subsidised loans. These developments indicate a shift towards debt financing for firms in the sectors most affected by AI. Turning to bond pricing, Chart 25a (left panel) shows that AI-exposed non-financial firms in the STOXX Europe 600 exhibit lower option-adjusted spreads than their non-exposed counterparts, although this pattern has reversed somewhat recently. In particular, both the median and interquartile range of spreads for AI-exposed firms have shifted downward in most years of the sample period. Concurrently, these firms have issued a larger share of bonds with maturities exceeding ten years, whereas non-exposed issuers exhibit a greater concentration of bonds at intermediate maturities. Checking for credit risk (Expected Default Frequency, leverage, profitability and size), bond characteristics and bond fixed effects, AI exposure is estimated to correspond to around 5 basis points tighter spreads (Chart 25a, right panel). This combination of lower spreads and longer maturities suggests more favourable debt financing conditions for AI-exposed firms, since longer maturities would typically be associated with higher spreads in the absence of such advantages. Taken together, these results indicate a modest but robust relation between AI exposure and a lower market-implied cost of debt financing. In relation to the equity market, AI-exposed firms recorded higher median annual stock returns than non-exposed firms in most years of the sample (Chart 25b, left panel). The upper part of the return distribution is also generally shifted upwards, suggesting that AI exposure has been associated not only with higher typical returns but also with some strong outperformers. AI-exposed firms also tend to trade at higher price-earnings ratios, consistent with investors assigning higher valuations to their expected future earnings and, potentially, with a longer-duration equity profile. The evidence also points to a robust equity-return premium to AI exposure of around 1.3 percentage points per quarter (Chart 25b, right panel). This finding does not appear to be driven by the technology sector, as excluding firms from that sector leaves the estimates virtually unchanged, nor by sector-wide AI rallies, since the spread differential persists when AI-exposed issuers are compared only with peers in the same sector and quarter. Turning to the banking sector, loans to euro area AI companies have been rising faster than loans to other sectors, although they still account for just under €200 billion. Banks allocate a relatively small share of their equity portfolio to AI companies outside of the euro area (the allocation to foreign AI firms in bank equity portfolios is below their market share in total global equities) (Chart 26a). [ 25 ] By contrast, banks overweight shares of euro area AI companies in their equity portfolios relative to their market share in the global equity basket, reflecting strong home bias in their equity holdings. The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. The banking sector is itself a significant AI adopter. Banks are increasingly deploying AI technologies to enhance cost efficiency. An LLM contextual analysis of bank earnings calls reveals that bank executives increasingly highlight their AI adoption plans in their interactions with investors (Chart 27a). Almost half of those references specifically focus on the potential benefits of AI in terms of cost optimisation and automation. More general remarks on broader AI adoption strategy are also mentioned relatively frequently. Mentions of the operational risk of cyber threat incidents in earnings calls remain more limited, standing in contrast with the evidence that banks are facing rising cybersecurity threats. Fast-advancing AI is widening the set of operational risks to which banks are exposed (Chart 27b). The rapid advancement of AI models is creating new cybersecurity challenges for banks by exposing previously hidden vulnerabilities. While it is difficult to elicit the share of threats that is exclusively related to the use of AI models, IT, cybersecurity and related incidents are already rising, accounting for 10-12 per cent of all operational risk events in 2025, nearly double their incidence in 2018. Recent evidence shows that cyberattacks affecting payment systems can prompt banks to tap their liquidity reserves or increase central bank borrowing. Cyberattacks on small banks can also disrupt local banking markets, as depositors and customers may shift activity away from affected institutions. This highlights how cyber risk can amplify liquidity and funding pressures, particularly for banks with limited cyber resources. Cyber risk is only a part of a broader set of operational risks that banks are currently facing. In general, losses from these risks remain contained, amounting to 0.9 per cent of aggregate capital in 2025. However, this masks substantial heterogeneity in the distribution of losses across significant institutions, with losses concentrated in tail events which may have repercussions for bank valuations, earnings expectations and, when large or interconnected institutions are hit, systemic risk. Recourse to debt financing by AI firms in the euro area increased recently (Chart 28a). Internal estimates suggest that the AI boom accounts for around 0.9 percentage points of additional aggregate annual credit growth – about one quarter of the total credit growth as of the first quarter of 2026. As is shown in Chart 28b, relative to the United States, equity markets in Europe are shallower, venture capital is less developed, and firms rely more heavily on debt financing – especially via banks – to scale up throughout their life cycle. Recourse to debt financing by AI firms increased recently, both for AI developers and AI adopters, strengthening aggregate firm debt dynamics. Since early 2025 and up to the first quarter of 2026, AI developers and AI adopters have increased their leverage by between 1 and 1.5 percentage points more than comparable firms that were not exposed to AI (Chart 29a). The increase in debt was more marked in the form of marketable debt than loans (Chart 29b). AI firms in general also tend to be more liquid than their non-AI peers (Chart 30). Among them, AI developers specialised in intangibles are more cash-rich, with cash ratios around 12 percentage points higher than those of comparable non-AI firms. AI infrastructure firms also display higher cash ratios than their non-AI peers, by around 5 percentage points. High cash reserves are consistent with their business models along two dimensions. First, AI infrastructure firms have high temporal mismatches between set-up costs and revenues, thus requiring higher precautionary liquidity buffers to operate. Second, high cash buffers allow them to improve balance sheet figures and potentially to better negotiate funding with financial institutions when this is needed to expand operations. AI adopters also tend to display higher cash by about 3 percentage points, relative to their peers, suggesting that stronger balance sheets are linked to AI adoption. Conclusions This speech has highlighted that AI is currently a significant contributor to growth in the euro area, driven by both expenditure on AI adoption and the role of European firms in the global AI supply chain. Surveys of firms and households indicate significant AI adoption rates, albeit unevenly distributed across sectors and demographic groups. A striking pattern is that European households are net positive about the employment impact of AI. However, the AI adoption process is still at a relatively early stage and the extent and timing of the economy-wide transformative potential of AI remain highly uncertain. The European financial system has responded to the external financing needs generated by increased AI activity, even if internal funding remains the most important source of funding. European investors are also major investors in foreign AI equities and the euro-denominated bond issuances by American hyperscalers, even if the latter are primarily funded by a lower allocation to US Treasury bonds. Looking ahead, tracking the near-term and medium-term implications of AI will remain high on the analytical agenda at the ECB. The SAFE results are broadly consistent with other surveys on AI adoption among firms. A European Commission survey conducted in 2026 Q1 finds that 42 per cent of European mid-caps and SMEs use AI or automated systems at work. Of these, 30 per cent use these tools only to a limited or experimental extent, and 12 per cent use them extensively. A further 21 per cent plan to adopt them, while 35 per cent neither use nor plan to use them. The most common applications are customer service (47 per cent), productivity monitoring (36 per cent) and logistics or staff scheduling (30 per cent). See European Commission (2026), “ Workplace-related drivers and obstacles for the adoption of AI ”, Eurobarometer, October, Brussels. The European Investment Bank Investment Report reports similar adoption rates: 46 per cent of EU firms used big data analytics or AI in 2025, and 49 per cent used digital platforms (European Investment Bank (2026), “ Investment Report 2025/26: Capitalising on Europe’s strengths ”, Investment Report , Luxembourg). Harmonised central bank business surveys for Germany, France and Italy (2024/2025) likewise show AI use spreading rapidly, with most firms still at an experimental or limited stage: Bencivelli, L., De Masi, L., Falck, E., Fernández Cerezo, A., Formai, S., Hidalgo Bricio, I., Mattevi, E. and Nagengast, A. (2026), “ Embracing AI in Europe: New evidence from harmonised central bank business surveys ”, VoxEU, 9 January. However, a survey of senior corporate executives in a number of countries indicates higher adoption rates (Yotzov, I., Barrero, J. M., Bloom, N., Bunn, P., Chawla, C., Davis, S. J., Foster, K. (2026), “ Firm Data on AI ”, NBER Working Paper , No. 34836, October). The same study shows that AI spending is highly concentrated: a small group of top spenders (around 2 per cent of firms) accounts for a large share of total expenditure. Among firms planning AI-related investment over the next 12 months, most expect to invest in AI-related technologies and tools, as well as in employee training, financed mostly through internal funds. 49 per cent of firms plan to invest in AI technologies and tools (e.g. software licences), 46 per cent in training employees, 40 per cent in data and infrastructure and 12 per cent in hiring AI specialists. See also: Ferrando, A., Lamboglia, S., Rariga, J. and Schmidt, M. (2026), “ Adopting and investing in AI: evidence from euro area firms in the SAFE ”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 2, ECB; Chaloupka, D., Lalinský, T. and Lopez-Garcia P. (2026), “ What separates firms that use AI intensively from firms that don’t? ”, The ECB Blog , ECB, 24 June. On how firms are financing AI, see: Cianfarani, A.S., Di Casola, P., Ramos, J. and Zander, D. (2026), “ Funding the AI revolution: evidence from euro area sectors ”, The ECB Blog , ECB, 6 October. Baumann, U., Cullen, Z., Faia, E., Ferrando, A., Perez-Truglia, R. and Rariga, J. (2026), “ Innovation without borders? The geography of technological diffusion ”, Working Paper Series , No. 3246, ECB, Frankfurt am Main. Dias da Silva, A., Lebastard, L. and Sondermann, D. (2026), “ AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report ”, The ECB Blog , ECB, 26 August. Compared to other surveys of employees, the level of AI adoption indicated by the Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) is at the upper end of the range. This may reflect its broad framing on question on AI usage. A recent survey finds that 32 per cent among European workers (Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden and the UK) use AI for their job: see Bick, A., Blandin, A., Deming, D. J., Fuchs,-Schündeln, N. and Jessen, J. (2026), “ Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S. ”, NBER Working Paper , No. 34995, March. This survey finds similar cross-sectional patterns as in the ECB CES survey: younger and more educated workers have higher AI adoption rates. According to the latest Eurostat data for 2025, 32.7 per cent of people aged 16-74 in the EU used generative AI tools, with about half of them using generative AI for work: see Eurostat (2026), “ Use of artificial intelligence by individuals ”, Statistics Explained , No. 145512, European Commission. Other surveys also point to positive but modest time savings. In a 2026 European Commission survey employed AI users report time savings of about 7.4 hours per month (4.6 per cent of working time): see European Commission, (2026), “ AI at work in Europe: Perceived impacts on productivity, quality of work, and job security ”, European Economy Technical Paper, No. 087, Directorate-General for Economic and Financial Affairs. The Bick et al. survey (2026, op. cit.) finds aggregate time savings of between 1.0 per cent and 1.8 per cent in the European countries in the sample. In a recent Danish survey, users report average time savings of 2.8 per cent of work hours: see Humlum, A. and Vestergaard, E. (2025), “ Still waters, rapid currents: Early labour market transformation under generative AI ”, NBER Working Papers , No. 33777, National Bureau of Economic Research. A recent LSE study finds similar estimates to those in the CES: see Jolles, D. and Lordan, G. (2025), “ Bridging the generational AI gap: Unlocking productivity for all generations ”, Research report, The Inclusion Initiative at the London School of Economics and Political Science. With respect to employment perceptions, other surveys support the evidence from the CES that euro area workers are, on balance, positive about how AI will affect their own jobs. In a 2024 Eurobarometer, 66 per cent of EU employees reported that AI and recent digital technologies benefit their work: see European Commission (2025), “ Artificial intelligence and the future of work ”, Special Eurobarometer , No. 554, February. Among employed AI users in a 2026 European Commission survey, about 60 per cent report no fear of losing their job because of AI, while 13.9 per cent are very concerned and 26.2 per cent somewhat concerned: see European Commission, Directorate-General for Economic and Financial Affairs. (2026), “ European Business Cycle Indicators: AI at work in Europe: Perceived impacts on productivity, quality of work, and job security ”, European Economy Technical Paper , No. 087. Views of respondents are also more negative about jobs in general than about their own job. In the same Eurobarometer survey, 66 per cent of respondents reported that AI and robots could take jobs rather than create them. Each bar is the GenAI exposure score of an average euro of pay in that industry, euro area, 2023. The scale runs from 0 (AI can do nothing of the job) to 1 (AI could do the whole job). The score comes from the ILO's task-based index (Gmyrek, P., Berg, J., Kaminski, K., Konopczynski, F., Ladna, A., Nafradi, B., Roslaniec, K. and Troszynski, M. (2025), “ Generative AI and Jobs ”, ILO Working Paper , No. 140, International Labour Office, Geneva). Detailed occupations are placed into industries using US occupation-by-industry data (US Bureau of Labour Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics), because the same broad occupation means different jobs in different industries: "professionals" are software developers in IT services but doctors and nurses in health care. The scores are weighted by earnings: Eurostat's Structure of Earnings Survey gives pay by occupation in each country and industry, and national accounts give each industry's weight in the wage bill. The simulation is run using the MANKIO model (Rubbo, E., Osbat, C., Buss, G., Cantelmo, A., Dobrew, M., Dominguez-Dıaz, R., Elfsbacka Schmöller, M., Gallegos, J.-E., Lisack, N., Pisani, M., Quintana Gonzalez, J. and Verdini, D. (2026), "Shock transmission in a monetary union: Aggregate impacts and cross-sectional incidence across EA countries", mimeo .) This is a multi-country, multi-industry model with sticky prices and monetary policy. The geographic regions are: 20 euro-area countries, the United States, an Asia-AI bloc (China, Japan, Korea) and the rest of the world. There are 75 industries per country from the FIGARO input-output tables, 2023. The experiment is as follows: Total factor productivity of the IT services industry (NACE J62-63: software, IT consulting, data services) rises by 30 per cent, everywhere in the world at once, as an unanticipated and near-permanent change. The 30 per cent shock is broadly in line with the 32.6 per cent gain in software-engineering productivity between November 2022 and December 2025 that can be inferred from stock prices (Blumenfeld, A., Hazell, J., Lian, C. and Schaab, A. (2026), “ The Macroeconomic Effect of AI: Sizing the Software Engineering Channel ”, NBER Working Paper , No. 35793, September). Since this study calculates the priced effect more than doubled by mid-2026, the 30 per cent scenario is just one scenario. Field experiments across three firms suggest that developers with AI tools completed 26 per cent more pull requests (Cui, K. Z., Demirer, M., Jaffe, S., Musolff, L., Peng, S. and Salz, T. (2026), “ The effects of generative AI on high-skilled work: evidence from three field experiments with software developers ”, forthcoming in Management Science . The inflation impact is limited: prices fall in the first year, then inflation returns to target and the policy rate is back near baseline. It is beyond the scope of this speech to assess the implications for credit dynamics and asset price dynamics if there were a shift in beliefs about the future economic impact of AI or if there were a shift in global risk appetite. Grant finance also plays a role. Haque, S., Kim, Y., Mayer, S. and Wu, E. (2026), “ Liquidity for Transformation: Bank Credit and Firms' AI Adoption ”, Social Sciences Research Network, No. 7247864. At the same time, these findings, as well as the lower cost of debt financing for AI-exposed firms, could also reflect market optimism about the benefits of AI which may turn out not to be fully warranted. Banks are minor investors in euro area AI equities, holding around €150 billion out of their €4.5 trillion market capitalisation. Investment funds also exhibit home bias in their equity portfolios but to a lesser degree than banks. See: Altavilla, C., Burlon, L., Kalemli-Özcan, S. and Ramos, J. (2026), “Monetary Policy, Segmented Capital Markets and Innovation”, (forthcoming in ECB working paper series ); Hartmann, P. and Maver, V. (2025), “ Implications of Artificial Intelligence for Monetary Policy – A First Conceptual Assessment ”, SUERF Policy Brief , No 1080, 30 January. The evidence indicates that sectors with high AI adoption potential see higher business formation rates. See Bena, J., Bian, B. and Giannetti, M. (2026), “ Prompted to start: how GenAI is transforming entrepreneurship ,” CEPR discussion paper no. 21282. title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
body: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals Scientists at the Allen Telescope Array have integrated the NVIDIA Holoscan platform to search for signals that may come from aliens — or the AI they built. October 30, 2026 by Chris Porter 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument. Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours. Science Fact, Not Fiction The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula. Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon. Learn more about NVIDIA AI for science . title: Seoul fears being sidelined as US reaches out to North Korea
body: Conflicts South Korea Seoul fears being sidelined as US reaches out to North Korea Julian Ryall 10/30/2026 October 30, 2026 With ties between South Korea and the Trump administration strained, the South Korean government worries that Donald Trump's pursuit of a diplomatic breakthrough with Kim Jong Un may come at Seoul's expense. https://p.dw.com/p/5OrjO Prefer DW on Google South Korea has been facing pressure both from North Korea and from its ally, the United States Image: Evan Vucci/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement South Korea 's relationship with the North, always strained, seems to be going through a particularly hostile patch in recent weeks. Last month, Seoul accused North Korea of planting a mine on the southern side of the heavily fortified border. The device exploded, injuring three South Korean soldiers . Pyongyang refused to apologize and insisted this was a false-flag incident designed to tarnish the isolated nation. The North Korean regime has since conducted multiple weapons tests , held its first-ever exhibition of military drones attended by Kim Jong Un, brought up self-propelled artillery units to the border and started preparing loudspeaker systems that will blast propaganda into the South. On Thursday, North Korea also fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the Sea of Japan just before a scheduled visit to South Korea by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz . On top of South Korea's issues with its arch rival, many in Seoul are growing increasingly wary of their most important ally, the United States. South Korean politicians are worried that the US could push for a diplomatic breakthrough with North Korea at the cost of ignoring South Korea's security , or even leave it exposed to Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal. Who gets a voice on South Korea's future? US President Donald Trump famously claimed he and Kim Jong Un "fell in love" during Trump's first term. More recently, Trump has indicated he would like to resume talks . There have been suggestions that a meeting could take place on November 18 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The North Korean side has made no official response to Washington's hints, although South Korea's National Intelligence Service informed a closed-door meeting of Seoul's intelligence committee on Thursday that Kim Jong Un discussed the possibility of meeting Trump when he met with senior members of China's politburo in Dandong on Saturday. Seoul's fears were also fueled by the US proposing three-way talks with Russia and China on the fate of Ukraine without inviting a representative of Kyiv to attend. The worry in Seoul is that President Donald Trump may conduct a similar bypass manoeuvre on the Korean Peninsula. Washington-Seoul relationship shaken by tariffs, funding disputes "Right now, there is a problem of trust between the two governments," said Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation. A security and trade relationship that was previously considered secure has been rocked by tariffs, trade restrictions and demands from Washington that the South pay more for the US troops stationed in the country, Kim told DW. President Lee's diplomats have lost access to key decision-making personnel in this White House, he added. "I do not think this US administration is thinking long-term in the relationship with South Korea," Kim said. "They do not see South Korea as a part of their wider national security network and I do not think they are listening to experts on the importance of allies in the region." "I also think that Trump is eager to meet with Kim because of his personal quest to obtain a Nobel Peace Prize." Trump's widely publicized efforts to secure a Nobel have been thwarted so far. However, this might change if Trump somehow manages to formally end the Korean War that was put on hold by the 1953 armistice. South Korea eyeing its own nuclear deterrent "The most serious concern is that the US recognizes Pyongyang as a nuclear power, which would legitimize the North's program and undermine efforts to convince it to abolish its nuclear weapons as well as the broader non-proliferation system," said Lim Eun-jung, a professor of international studies at Kongju National University. In parallel, she said, there are fears that Trump could reach an agreement with North Korea that requires it to scrap its long-range nuclear missiles — those that are capable of hitting targets in the United States — but permits it to retain short-range weapons that can still easily reach South Korea and Japan. That would raise questions about the US commitment to defend South Korea in case of a nuclear attack. That uncertainty, in turn, is likely to give credence to voices arguing that South Korea needs to develop its own nuclear deterrent. "For years, we have depended on US extended deterrence guarantees under the nuclear umbrella, but this US administration is unpredictable and there are more and more people asking why we don't just go it alone," Lim told DW. "Virtually, all our neighbors have nuclear weapons, and while no-one wants the dominoes to start falling, it could happen." Merz says Korean security affects Europe The latest escalation between Seoul and Pyongyang comes amid repeated attempts by South Korean President Lee to improve communication with Pyongyang . The perceived outreach has irritated South Korea's European allies , who are angry over North Korea deploying soldiers and supplying munition and missiles to help Russia in the Ukraine war . Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Moscow is believed to be repaying Pyongyang's support with money, military technology and security guarantees. During his visit to South Korea , Germany's Merz pointed out that "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects the security of Korea." "The world is small — even in war," Merz added. South Korea needs allies Berlin, just like Seoul, has been disoriented by the Trump administration turning hostile on many of its allies while seeking reproachment with geopolitical rivals such as Russia and China. During his Asia tour, Merz pushed for an alliance of middle powers to protect free trade and oppose "unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law." German Chancellor Merz recently visited South Korea along with Japan and Singapore Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance "The fact remains that the United States is shifting its foreign policy, ⁠its foreign economic ​policy, and redefining its interests. As they do so, we must do the same," he said in South Korea. It was not clear if Seoul will respond to Merz's appeal by moving closer to the European Union . At the moment, however, it seems apparent that the South Korean government is struggling to communicate with either North Korea or the US. "It is a very difficult situation," said Kim Sang-woo. "There is no trust and no connections and that, to me, is very worrisome." Advertisement

body:
Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates) Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates) October 2026 30 October 2026 External communication ECB President Lagarde to step down on 7 February 2027 On 29 October 2026 ECB President Christine Lagarde informed the Governing Council and the President of the European Council António Costa that she would step down from her position on 7 February 2027. A related press release was published on the ECB’s website on the same day. Market infrastructure and payments T2 Currency Participation Agreements (CPAs) with Sveriges Riksbank and Danmarks Nationalbank On 21 October 2026 the Governing Council approved the T2 CPA on the use of T2 services by Sveriges Riksbank, following a positive assessment by the Market Infrastructure Board regarding the onboarding of Sveriges Riksbank to T2. The Governing Council also approved an updated T2 CPA on the use of T2 services by Danmarks Nationalbank to implement changes applicable to all CPAs that were introduced during the onboarding of Sveriges Riksbank. Both agreements were subsequently signed by the respective parties. Advice on legislation ECB Opinion on empowering the competent authority under the market abuse regulation to impose a ban on exercising management functions in credit institutions On 1 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/30 at the request of the Belgian Minister for Finances and Pensions, in charge of the National Lottery and the Federal Cultural Institutions. ECB Opinion on the governance structure and conflict of interest rules of the Central Bank of Cyprus On 8 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/31 at the request of the Central Bank of Cyprus, in agreement with the Cypriot Ministry of Finance. ECB Opinion on the right to use cash, access to cash, electronic means of payment, and free payment services On 8 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/32 at the request of the Slovenian Ministry of Finance. Corporate governance Amendments to legal instruments related to the Eurosystem accounting and financial reporting framework On 22 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Guideline ECB/2026/28 amending Guideline (EU) 2024/2941 on the legal framework for accounting and financial reporting in the European System of Central Banks (ECB/2024/31). The amending Guideline, which will be published on EUR-Lex in due course, enhances transparency regarding the Eurosystem’s financial performance via a new reporting format for the consolidated annual balance sheet of the Eurosystem that requires changes to the categorisation of content under the items “Sundry”, “Reserves”, “Accumulated losses carried forward” and “Profit/(loss) for the year”. Appointment of the Chair of the Legal Committee (LEGCO) On 29 October 2026 the Governing Council appointed Petra Senkovic, ECB Director General Legal Services as of 1 November 2026, as Chair of LEGCO as of that date. Ms Senkovic will succeed Chiara Zilioli, who is retiring from the ECB. This appointment runs until 31 December 2028 to coincide with the terms of office of the chairs of the other Eurosystem/ESCB committees, who were reappointed in November 2025 for a three-year period from January 2026 to December 2028. International and European cooperation Extension of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) cooperation programme for strengthening the central bank capacities in the Western Balkans to the central banks of Moldova and Ukraine On 8 October 2026 the Governing Council supported the extension of the ongoing third phase of the cooperation programme between the ESCB and the Western Balkans to also include the central banks of Moldova and Ukraine, and endorsed the related legal and contractual documentation. This cooperation programme, coordinated by the Deutsche Bundesbank and financed by the European Commission under its Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance (IPA III) Programming Framework for the period 2021-27, involves 21 ESCB national central banks and the third phase started in 2026 for a three-year period. As a result, the Western Balkans Phase III programme will consist of two regional components: the “Regional Component Moldova and Ukraine” and the “Regional Component WB6” for the ongoing programme for the Western Balkans. title: Two Men Sentenced for Acting as Agents of the People’s Republic of China
body: Press Release Two Men Sentenced for Acting as Agents of the People’s Republic of China Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Defendants Facilitated Secret Cash Payments and Targeted U.S. Military  Personnel on Behalf of the PRC’s Ministry of State Security Two nationals of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) were sentenced today for conspiring to act as agents of the PRC government and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General. Liren “Ryan” Lai, 40, and Yuance Chen, 39, were each sentenced to 30 months in prison and three years of supervised release. The defendants agreed to operate under the direction and control of the PRC’s Ministry of State Security (MSS), carrying out clandestine intelligence activities in the United States that included facilitating secret “dead drop” cash payments in exchange for information related to the national security of the United States, gathering information about U.S. military personnel and installations, and assisting efforts to recruit potential intelligence assets from within the U.S. military. “Liren Lai and Yuance Chen operated in a long-running scheme to undermine U.S. national security by supporting Chinese intelligence operations and recruiting in the United States,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Lai’s and Chen’s activities, undertaken at the direction of the PRC, were extensive and brazen. The National Security Division is committed to holding accountable anyone who aids or abets such espionage efforts.” “These defendants were directed by a foreign intelligence service to gather information about the U.S. military in the hopes of undermining our national security,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “This office and our federal law enforcement partners stand watch day and night to prevent our adversaries from doing just that, and we will continue to do so. There are many nations around the world that wish this country ill.  And today’s sentences should demonstrate our commitment to holding accountable anyone who poses a similar threat to our nation.” “By their own admission, Chen and Lai operated as illegal agents for the Chinese government on U.S. soil, carrying out clandestine intelligence work that included making covert payments, collecting sensitive military information, and attempting to recruit American service members,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The Chinese government’s efforts to infiltrate our armed forces demonstrate just how far it will go to threaten U.S. national security, but it has underestimated the FBI’s commitment to thwarting its illegal activity and holding its agents accountable. Let this sentencing serve as a clear warning: If you attempt to jeopardize the safety and security of our service members, our citizens, or our nation, justice will find you.” According to court documents, Lai and Chen began acting as agents of the MSS no later than May 2021. The MSS is the PRC’s principal civilian intelligence service, responsible for conducting foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations. Lai recruited Chen into the scheme and initially served as an intermediary between Chen and MSS intelligence officers. Chen subsequently received assignments directly from MSS officers. As detailed in the government’s sentencing memorandum, Lai and Chen facilitated a clandestine cash payment of approximately $10,000 in January 2022. While the defendants were in the PRC, they coordinated with individuals in the United States to leave a backpack containing the cash in a locker at a recreational facility in Livermore, Calif. Such arrangements, known as “dead drops,” allow intelligence operatives to transfer money or information without directly meeting the intended recipient. The defendants’ illegal activities extended beyond facilitating covert payments on behalf of the MSS. Beginning in 2022, Chen gathered information about U.S. military installations and personnel at the direction of Lai and MSS intelligence officers. These activities included obtaining photographs of Navy Base Kitsap in Bremerton, Wash., and photographs and videos of military recruits and active-duty sailors inside a Navy recruiting station in Southern California. Chen also collected personal identifying information about a U.S. Navy employee and maintained detailed biographical information about military personnel who were potential intelligence targets. In March 2023, Lai traveled to the U.S. and delivered a cell phone to Chen for covert communications with the MSS referred to by Chen as a “state secret.”  Chen later traveled to China in 2024 and 2025, where he met with MSS officers and received additional assignments concerning U.S. service members. In April 2025, Lai again traveled from China to the U.S. to carry out assignments for the MSS. The following month, the MSS directed him to travel to Phoenix to facilitate another clandestine cash payment of approximately $20,000 in furtherance of its intelligence operations. Lai and Chen were arrested on June 27, 2025, during a coordinated FBI counterintelligence and law enforcement operation. A federal grand jury in the Northern District of California returned an indictment on July 1, 2025, charging both defendants with conspiracy to act as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification. Lai pleaded guilty to both offenses on Dec. 12, 2025. Chen pleaded guilty to both offenses on Feb. 20. The FBI San Francisco Field Office led the investigation, with assistance from the FBI’s Portland, Houston, and San Diego Field Offices and the Naval Criminal Investigative Service. The National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California handled the prosecution of the case. Significant operational support and assistance was also provided by the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the District of Oregon, the Southern District of Texas, and the Southern District of California. Updated October 30, 2026 Topic National Security Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) National Security Division (NSD) USAO - California, Northern Press Release Number: 26-1301

title: Gun-Toting Felon Who Ran from Officers  Sentenced to Federal Prison
body: Press Release Gun-Toting Felon Who Ran from Officers  Sentenced to Federal Prison Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Iowa A felon who ran from officers and dropped a gun was sentenced today to more than two years in federal prison.  Darrell Jawon Wilson, age 19, from Cedar Rapids, Iowa, received the prison term after an April 13, 2026, guilty plea to possession of a firearm by a felon. Evidence at a prior court hearing showed that on October 1, 2025, in Waterloo, Iowa, officers went to a liquor store because of a report that two men wearing masks were walking around the area and looking in cars.  Officers arrived and located the two men.  One man, later identified as Wilson, ran.  An officer chased him and saw him pull out a gun from his waistline.  Wilson fell and dropped the gun.  After Wilson was taken into custody, officers retraced the path of the pursuit and found the gun.  Wilson has felony convictions for conspiracy to commit a forcible felony and going armed with intent. Wilson was sentenced in Cedar Rapids by United States District Court Chief Judge C.J. Williams.  Wilson was sentenced to 27 months’ imprisonment and must also serve a three-year term of supervised release after the prison term.  There is no parole in the federal system. This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Devra T. Hake and was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and the Waterloo Police Department. Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl . The case file number is 25-CR-2067. Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA. title: Leader of South Georgia Check‑Theft and Forgery Scheme Sentenced to Prison
body: Press Release Leader of South Georgia Check‑Theft and Forgery Scheme Sentenced to Prison Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Georgia Defendant Led $115K Fraud Using Stolen Checks and Facebook Recruits ALBANY, Ga. – A Thomasville, Georgia, man who directed a $115,000 check theft and forgery scheme in the region has been sentenced to federal prison. “Stealing checks and forging financial documents is not a victimless crime. These types of schemes siphon money from hardworking individuals and local businesses, causing real financial harm across our communities,” said U.S. Attorney William R. “Will” Keyes. “Thanks to the outstanding work of our federal and local law enforcement partners, this conspiracy has been dismantled, and those responsible are being held accountable.” “The sentencings demonstrate the U.S. Postal Inspection Service's dedication to safeguarding the nation's mail system by partnering with our law enforcement partners to combat mail theft,” said Rodney M. Hopkins, Inspector in Charge of the Atlanta Division. “Let this be a warning: if you abuse the U.S. Postal Service and exploit the public’s trust for personal gain then you will be held accountable.” De'Andre Kenterrious L. McClarin, 28, of Thomasville, was sentenced to serve 60 months in prison to be followed by five years of supervised release on October 28, after he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit bank fraud on Dec. 30, 2025. Danmon Jerone Wilkerson, 25, of Tallahassee, Florida, was sentenced to serve 27 months in prison to be followed by five years of supervised release on October 28, after he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit bank fraud on March 19. In addition, the defendants were ordered to pay a combined total of $115,936.05 restitution. Six other co-conspirators, with varying levels of involvement in the scheme, were charged federally, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, and sentenced: Kemareon Bryant, 28, of Thomasville, was sentenced to serve 18 months in prison and three years of supervised release on June 18. Jerry Hayes, 54, of Thomasville, was sentenced to serve 12 months and one day in prison and three years of supervised release on Nov. 20, 2025. Jaylen Filmore, 24, of Thomasville, was sentenced to serve one day in prison and three years of supervised release on May 28. Jelan Hayes, 28, of Thomasville, was sentenced to serve one day in prison and three years of supervised release on September 3. Angela Cookley, 25, of Tallahassee, Florida, was sentenced to time served and three years of supervised release on June 18. Kembrick McClendon, 37, of Thomasville, was sentenced to time served and three years of supervised release on August 20. Senior U.S. District Judge W. Louis Sands presided over the case. There is no parole in the federal system. According to court documents and statements made in court, investigators discovered that McClarin, beginning in January 2022, used a stolen postal key to break into USPS mail receptacles and collection boxes, stealing checks and check information. McClarin would edit the checks and even use a check printer to produce fraudulent checks. McClarin recruited people to participate in the fraud, often on Facebook, by sharing their own personal and bank information to enable him to deposit the stolen and forged checks into their bank accounts and withdraw the money. Wilkerson was one of these individuals who shared personal and bank information to participate in the scheme, including setting up an account at JP Morgan Chase Bank. Other financial institutions targeted in the scheme included Truist, Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Synovus, U.S. Bank, Prime Meridian, Bank of America, Capital City Bank, Centennial Bank, Peoples South Bank, Ameris, VyStar Credit Union, Navy Federal Credit Union, and TC Federal Credit Union. Agents ultimately determined that the McClarin-led conspiracy caused $115,936.05 in losses to the banks and credit unions. The United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) and the Thomas County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case, with valuable assistance from the Thomasville Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Hannah Couch prosecuted case for the Government with assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Christian Bryant and Criminal Chief Leah McEwen. title: Botox Fraud Doctor Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison for $45M Medicare Scheme
body: Press Release Botox Fraud Doctor Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison for $45M Medicare Scheme Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs California doctor Violetta Mailyan was sentenced yesterday to 15 years in prison for using her medical practice to fraudulently bill Medicare more than $45 million for Botox injection services that were medically unnecessary and never provided. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Violetta Mailyan, 45, of Glendale, California, owned and operated Healthy Way Medical Center, a clinic that purported to provide beauty and cosmetic services. Although Medicare reimburses medical providers for Botox injections when necessary to treat documented cases of chronic migraines, Mailyan billed and received payments for thousands of injections that were never provided, were provided only for cosmetic purposes, or were given to patients whose primary care physicians had not referred them for treatment of chronic migraines. Evidence also showed that Mailyan billed for thousands of injections, representing over $19 million, purportedly provided on days when her clinic was closed. Mailyan also billed for providing Botox injections when she was actually on vacation in Mexico, Hawaii, Las Vegas, Pennsylvania, and New York at various times throughout her fraud scheme. For example, Mailyan billed over $200,000 for purportedly providing Botox services to patients in California when she was actually relaxing on the beach in Cabo: Photograph from Mailyan’s Phone, Sent from Cabo, Mexico, the Same Day She Billed Medicare $34,560 For Services Purportedly Rendered in Glendale, California The evidence also showed that when Mailyan realized federal investigators were closing in, she tried to hide her tracks by falsifying medical records and forging Medicare beneficiary signatures, including for a man who was in federal prison during the time Mailyan claimed to have provided treatment. Mailyan submitted these records to federal investigators, intending to throw them off her trail and make it appear as though she had seen patients she had not actually seen. Mailyan used the money she stole to purchase luxury goods, including a $12,000 17th century crossbow and a $3,000 painting, depicted below: 17th Century Crossbow and $3,000 Painting that Mailyan Purchased with Medicare Fraud Proceeds In sentencing Mailyan, the Court commented that Mailyan’s fraud “was truly breathtaking in scope and shocking in its duration,” and that her actions were “almost unbelievable in their brazenness.” In addition to the prison sentence, the Court ordered the immediate forfeiture of over $16,029,742 worth of property seized from Mailyan, including real property, personal property, securities, and bank funds, effectively returning this taxpayer money to the United States. Mailyan was also ordered to pay $32,904,049.41 in restitution to Medicare, and the United States will vigorously pursue the return of these stolen funds. After a six-day jury trial ending in May 2026, Mailyan was convicted of nine counts of wire fraud and three counts of obstruction of a criminal investigation of a health care offense. The jury also found that Mailyan used the fraud proceeds to purchase two Tesla vehicles, including a Cybertruck, and five pieces of California real estate. HHS-OIG and FBI investigated the case. Trial Attorneys Sandor Callahan and Jeffrey A. Crapko of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section prosecuted the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Tara Vavere for the Central District of California’s Asset Forfeiture and Recovery Section is handling asset forfeiture matters. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit . Updated October 30, 2026 Topic Fraud Component National Fraud Enforcement Division Press Release Number: 26-1304
retained_feed_body: California doctor Violetta Mailyan was sentenced yesterday to 15 years in prison for using her medical practice to fraudulently bill Medicare more than $45 million for Botox injection services that were medically unnecessary and never provided.

title: Homeland Security Task Force:  Two Connecticut Men Found with 21 Kilos of Cocaine Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison
body: Press Release Homeland Security Task Force:  Two Connecticut Men Found with 21 Kilos of Cocaine Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Connecticut David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, today announced that REGINALD ROGERS 38, of Woodbridge, and LESTER ARRINGTON, 34, of Naugatuck, have each been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Stefan R. Underhill in Bridgeport to 120 months of imprisonment and five years of supervised release for trafficking cocaine.  Rogers was sentenced today and Arrington was sentenced on October 27. According to court documents and statements made in court, as part of a Homeland Security Task Force investigation, on February 23, 2026, Connecticut State Police troopers stopped a 2024 Subaru Crosstrek in Trumbull.  Rogers was driving the vehicle and Arrington was a passenger.  A K9 sniff of the vehicle alerted for the presence of narcotics, and a subsequent search revealed approximately 21 kilograms of cocaine hidden in two compartments (“traps”) that were installed under each front seat.  Rogers and Arrington were arrested on state charges at that time. Rogers and Arrington each pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine.  Each is released on a $150,000 bond and they are required to report to prison on January 13. Arrington and Rogers agreed to the forfeiture of the vehicle. This investigation was led by the Drug Enforcement Administration with the assistance of the Bridgeport, Danbury, Stamford, and Stratford Police Departments.  The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Justyn P. Stokely and Lauren C. Clark. This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion.  The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad.  Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement toward identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders.  In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF New Haven comprises agents and officers from the FBI, DEA, HSI, ATF, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation, U.S. Department of Transportation – Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Labor – Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Commerce – Bureau of Industry and Security’s Office of Export Enforcement, and Connecticut State Police, with prosecutions led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Connecticut. Updated October 30, 2026 Topics Homeland Security Task Force Asset Forfeiture Drug Trafficking Component USAO - Connecticut

title: Dominican National Pleads Guilty to Receiving Over $24,000 in SNAP Benefits
body: Press Release Dominican National Pleads Guilty to Receiving Over $24,000 in SNAP Benefits Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts BOSTON – A Boston man, who was born in the Dominican Republic and is a Lawful Permanent Resident, pleaded guilty today in federal court in Boston to stealing the identity of a U.S. citizen from Puerto Rico and using the stolen identity to obtain more than $20,000 in federally funded benefits from Massachusetts. Erpawi Roque Collado, 54, pleaded guilty to unlawfully obtaining Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits and theft of government money. U.S. District Court Judge Brian E. Murphy scheduled sentencing for Jan. 14, 2027. Collado was indicted on April 23, 2026. Collado used a stolen identity to obtain $24,128 in SNAP benefits from Massachusetts between December 2016 and May 2025. The charge of unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The charge of theft of government money provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Suzanne Sullivan Jacobus of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case. Updated October 30, 2026 Topics Benefit Fraud Immigration Component USAO - Massachusetts

title: Fifth Alien Charged for Illegally Voting in Nevada
body: Press Release Fifth Alien Charged for Illegally Voting in Nevada Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nevada LAS VEGAS – An Argentine national was charged today for illegally voting in the 2024 general election in Clark County, Nevada. “As this additional case demonstrates, there is a catastrophic failure to protect the ballot box,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “Every single illegal vote directly questions the very security of our elections and compromises public trust in our democratic processes. Our will enforce a zero-tolerance policy, and every single 611 case will be prosecuted to the absolute fullest extent of the law. We will aggressively hunt down and dismantle any attempts to compromise this election, and we will ensure that the voice of every lawful American citizen is completely protected from being diluted, neutralized, or stolen by illegal votes.” “Federal election laws are clear, and efforts to circumvent them will be investigated,” said Erin Burke, Special Agent in Charge for HSI Los Angeles. “HSI and our FBI partners will continue to identify and investigate alleged violations of federal election law, protect the integrity of the electoral process and ensure that those accused of criminal conduct are held accountable through the judicial process.” According to the criminal information, on or about November 5, 2024, Mariela Delia Mendoza, an Argentine national and a lawful permanent resident of the United States living in Las Vegas, illegally voted in an election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Member of the Senate, and Member of the House of Representatives. She was not a United States citizen. Mendoza is charged with one count of voting by an alien. The maximum statutory penalty is one year of imprisonment, a fine of up to $100,000, or both. An initial appearance date has not yet been scheduled. The FBI and HSI investigated this case. In addition to Mendoza, this month, the U.S. Attorney’s Office has charged four individuals for illegally voting, bringing the total in Nevada to five federally charged for illegal voting. These charges reflect the Department of Justice’s commitment to protecting the integrity of federal elections and ensuring that only eligible U.S. citizens participate in them. Jullie Ann Sumalinog Moore, from the Philippines and a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien for allegedly illegally voting in the 2024 General Election. Moneir Elzobier Ali Yousif, from Sudan and a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien for allegedly illegally voting in the 2024 General Election. Khalida Safi, from Afghanistan and a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien for allegedly illegally voting the 2024 General Election. Mlebinge Riziki Ramadhani, from the Democratic Republic of Congo and lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by an alien for allegedly illegally voted in the 2022 General Election. An information is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ### Updated October 30, 2026 Topic Voting and Elections Component USAO - Nevada

title: Justice Department Announces Final Rule Allowing Federal Firearms Licensees to Voluntarily Use NICS for Employee Background Checks
body: Press Release Justice Department Announces Final Rule Allowing Federal Firearms Licensees to Voluntarily Use NICS for Employee Background Checks Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs OAG Today, the Department of Justice announced a final rule authorizing Federal Firearms Licensees (FFLs) to voluntarily use the FBI's National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) to conduct background checks on certain current and prospective employees. “Firearms dealers deserve the confidence of knowing their employees are right with the law,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “This common-sense change delivers quick and clear background checks for firearms dealers based on the latest FBI information. The Trump Administration will always protect the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding gun owners.” “Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this FBI will always protect the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding gun owners,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “This is a common-sense change that appropriately expedites and clarifies the background check process for firearms dealers, and I want to thank our partners for working with us to make it happen.” The final rule implements a provision of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act , which directed the Attorney General to issue these regulations. Participation is optional for FFLs and requires the written consent of the employee. Under the final rule, an FFL may submit Firearm Handler Background Checks (FHCs) of eligible employees. Eligible employees include firearm handlers, employees of licensed manufacturers who have access to unfinished firearm components or manufacturing tools, and independent contractors or agents whose employment duties for an FFL allow them access to firearms, ammunition, or their manufacturing components. Those listed as responsible persons of FFLs are not eligible employees because they already undergo background checks through the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Until now, Department of Justice regulations prohibited FFLs from contacting NICS for any purpose other than a proposed firearm transfer. NICS will search the same databases it does for a firearm transfer: the NICS Indices, the National Crime Information Center, and the Interstate Identification Index. The FFL will receive a NICS Transaction Number and one of three responses: "Pass," "Pending," or "Did Not Pass." FFLs will not receive any of the subject’s underlying record information. A "Did Not Pass" response does not prohibit an FFL from employing the person in a position that does not involve access to firearms or ammunition. Generally, an FFL may conduct one FHC per eligible employee every 12 months, unless the FFL has reasonable cause to believe the employee has become subject to a potentially prohibiting event. The FBI will not charge a fee for these checks. A subject whose FHC received a "Did Not Pass" response may request the reason for the response and may appeal that response in the same manner and to the same extent as a person who is denied a firearm transfer. The final rule addresses applicable public comments received on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that was published in December 2024. The final rule takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives will issue separate guidance to FFLs on how to document FHCs. Updated October 30, 2026 Components Office of the Attorney General Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Press Release Number: 26-1303

title: Three Indicted for Violations of the Federal Controlled Substances Act Resulting in Death
body: Press Release Three Indicted for Violations of the Federal Controlled Substances Act Resulting in Death Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA –United States Attorney David I. Courcelle announced that IVORY CARTER (“CARTER”) age 44 , DONNISHA BROWN (“BROWN”) age 42 , AND CHRISTOPHER LEHMANN (“LEHMANN”) age 30, were charged in a recently unsealed four-count indictment on October 1, 2026. Count One charged CARTER , BROWN , and LEHMANN with conspiracy to distribute fentanyl resulting in death, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 841(a)(1), 841(b)(1)(C), and 846. Count Two charged LEHMANN with distribution of a controlled substance to a pregnant individual, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Sections 861(f), 841(a)(1), 841(b)(1)(C), and Title 18, United States Code, Section 2. Count Three charged CARTER with possession with intent to distribute controlled substances, in violation of Title 21, United States Code, Section 841(a)(1) and 841(b)(1)(C). Count Four charged LEHMANN with being an accessory after the fact, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 3. According to court records, beginning on a date unknown, but at least by December 27, 2025 and continuing to on or about December 28, 2025, in the Eastern District of Louisiana, CARTER , BROWN , and LEHMANN did knowingly and intentionally conspire to distribute a quantity of fentanyl to an individual, whose serious bodily injury and death resulted from the use of the substance. If convicted of Count One, CARTER faces a term of imprisonment of life and a fine of up to $1,000,000.00. If convicted of Count Three, CARTER faces a term of imprisonment of up to twenty years, a fine of up to $1,000,000.00, and at least three years of supervised release. If convicted of Count One, BROWN and LEHMANN face a term of imprisonment of no less than twenty years, a fine of up to $1,000,000.00 and at least three years of supervised release. If convicted of Count Four, LEHMANN faces a term of imprisonment of up to fifteen years. The defendants also face payment of a $100 mandatory special assessment fee per count. U.S. Attorney Courcelle reiterated that the indictment is merely a charging document and that the guilt of the defendant must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The case was investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration and the St. Charles Parish Sheriff’s Office.  The prosecution is being handled by Assistant United States Attorney Briana Williams of the Narcotics Unit. title: Former Turkey Leg Hut owner sentenced for role in arson-for-hire scheme
body: Press Release Former Turkey Leg Hut owner sentenced for role in arson-for-hire scheme Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Texas HOUSTON – A Houston businessman has been ordered to federal prison for conspiring to commit arson of a commercial building. Lyndell Leroy Price, 44, pleaded guilty June 11. U.S. District Judge Sim Lake ordered Price to serve 105 months in federal prison to be immediately followed by three years of supervised release. In handing down the sentence, the court noted that Price directed the arson of Bar 5015 without any regard for the safety of those who live nearby or the damage the explosion and fire would have on neighboring businesses. Judge Lake stated Price’s lack of respect for the law warranted a high sentence as a measure of deterrence and to protect the community. As part of his plea, Price admitted he directed others to intentionally set fire to Bar 5015, a Houston business his former partner owned on Almeda Road in Houston. Shortly before the fire, court records show that the owner had declined Price’s offer to buy into the bar and refused to sell his interest in the Turkey Leg Hut, an establishment he co-owned with Price’s estranged wife. In the early morning hours of June 12, 2020, the conspirators bought gasoline and gas cans before going to an area near the business. Wearing face coverings and carrying gasoline-filled containers, they walked to Bar 5015, poured gasoline across the entrance ramp and deck, ignited it, and fled. The fire caused significant damage to the business and endangered nearby occupied homes, commercial properties, and the electrical grid. After the arson, a member of the conspiracy called Price to report that the mission was complete. The conspirators then received payment from Price for their roles in the crime. John Lee Price, 39, Armani Williams, 28, Miziah Shepherd, 28, and Javon Harris, 27, all of Houston, previously pleaded guilty to the same charge and will be sentenced at a later date. Lyndell will remain in custody pending transfer to a Federal Bureau of Prisons facility to be determined in the near future. FBI – Houston; Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives; and Houston Fire Department Arson Bureau conducted the investigation with assistance of Houston Police Department, Texas Department of Public Safety, and Harris County Constable’s Office – Precinct 4. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sebastian A. Edwards and Keri Fuller prosecuted the case. Updated October 30, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Component USAO - Texas, Southern

title: Augusta Woman Pleads Guilty to Social Security Fraud
body: Press Release Augusta Woman Pleads Guilty to Social Security Fraud Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maine Deborah Oldis concealed assets and resources to obtain Social Security benefits BANGOR, Maine: An Augusta woman pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in Bangor to social security benefit fraud. According to court records, from about October 2018 to April 2022, Deborah Oldis , 63, intentionally concealed and failed to disclose her ownership of assets, including bonds, stocks, and a personal bank account. These assets would have rendered her ineligible to receive Social Security benefits or would have reduced the benefits she was due. As a result of her actions, Oldis received an overpayment of $34,540 in benefits. Oldis faces up to five years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, and up to three years of supervised release. She will be sentenced after the completion of a presentence investigative report by the U.S. Probation Office. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General investigated the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. ### Contact Alisa Ross, Assistant United States Attorney (Tel: 207-945-0373) Updated October 30, 2026 Topic Benefit Fraud Component USAO - Maine

title: District of Arizona Responds to Allegations of Non-Citizen Voter Registration
body: Press Release District of Arizona Responds to Allegations of Non-Citizen Voter Registration Friday, October 30, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Arizona PHOENIX, Ariz. – Today, U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine announced that his office has opened a case into recent reporting about three non-profit organizations registering non-citizens to vote in Arizona. The United States Attorney’s Office has already referred the matter to the FBI for a thorough federal investigation. On Monday, Oct. 26, U.S. Attorney Courchaine also sent letters to the Maricopa County Recorder and Arizona Secretary of State, expressing concerns about the recent reporting and encouraging those offices to review voter registrations associated with the accused non-profit organizations. On the eve of an important midterm election, the District of Arizona reminds the public that voting is limited solely to U.S. citizens. If you are a non-citizen, you may not vote in Tuesday’s election, even if you have legal authority to be in the country on a visa or as a legal permanent resident. Further, knowingly causing another person to be registered to vote while knowing that person is not entitled to do so would violate federal law.
